explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. David says, "Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength." (Psalm 29:1) He says it twice, like he really wants it to land. Heavenly beings get the first assignment in this psalm, and it's a big one.

Nice guess, since gold is what most of us think of when we hear "giving to a king." But David doesn't mention gold or silver anywhere here. He tells the heavenly beings to "…ascribe to the LORD glory and strength." (Psalm 29:1) Glory and strength are what he calls on them to ascribe to Him, and you can't pack those in a cookie box.

I can see why you'd pick that, because it sounds like temple talk. But in this verse David doesn't ask for sacrifices or offerings at all. He tells the heavenly beings to ascribe to the LORD "…glory and strength." (Psalm 29:1) It's about what they say of Him.
Right on, baker. David says, "The voice of the LORD is over the waters…" (Psalm 29:3) That's the first place he names. The psalm goes on to name more, like Lebanon and the Wilderness of Kadesh.

Sinai is a famous mountain, so I get the pull. But this psalm never mentions it. David says the voice of the LORD is "…over the waters…" (Psalm 29:3) He's got other places on his list, but Sinai isn't one of them.

Jerusalem is a big deal, friend, so it's a fair guess. But David doesn't name it here. The place he gives in this verse is "…over the waters…" (Psalm 29:3) The temple comes up later, in verse 9, but this verse is all about the waters.

That's the pair, baker. David says, "The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is majestic." (Psalm 29:4) Two lines, two words, and both of them are big. He doesn't stop to explain either one.

Deep sounds right for thunder, I'll give you that. But David doesn't call the voice distant, and he doesn't use "deep" either. He says it's "powerful" and "majestic." (Psalm 29:4) Those are the two words he gives it, and he leaves it right there.

Thunder does feel swift and sudden, so I see how you got there. But those aren't David's words. He says, "The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is majestic." (Psalm 29:4) Same voice, just described a different way.

Yes, friend, "The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars…" (Psalm 29:5) The next line says it again with a bigger word: "the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon." Cedars are tough trees, and they still don't hold up against that voice.

I see where that came from, since we just heard about the waters. But the verse says the voice of the LORD "…breaks the cedars…" (Psalm 29:5) Nothing gets watered here. Those cedars go through a lot more than a drink.

Plants is a gentle word, and this verse isn't gentle. David says the voice of the LORD "…breaks the cedars…" and then "the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon." (Psalm 29:5) Nobody's gardening in this psalm, friend.
That's the one, baker. "The voice of the LORD strikes with flames of fire." (Psalm 29:7) The psalm just keeps stacking up pictures of that voice. Thunder, then trees, then mountains, then fire.

Hail would fit a storm, so I follow you. But David doesn't mention hailstones in this psalm. He says the voice of the LORD "…strikes with flames of fire." (Psalm 29:7) Fire, friend. Not ice falling out of the sky, FIRE.

Rain would make sense with all that thunder. But the psalm never says it rains. What it says is that the voice of the LORD "…strikes with flames of fire." (Psalm 29:7) Fire is the picture in this verse, friend.
You got it, baker. David says, "The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness; the LORD shakes the Wilderness of Kadesh." (Psalm 29:8) Notice he says it twice. Even the wilderness gets shaken.

Sinai is a name a lot of folks know, so I get it. But David doesn't use it in this verse. The wilderness he names is Kadesh: "the LORD shakes the Wilderness of Kadesh." (Psalm 29:8) Save Sinai for another day.

Shur is a real wilderness in the Bible (Exodus 15:22), so you know your deserts, and that's not nothing. But David names a different one here: "the LORD shakes the Wilderness of Kadesh." (Psalm 29:8) I know, desert names run together like dough in a hot oven, so mixing them up is no crime, friend.

Yes, baker. "The LORD sits enthroned over the flood…" (Psalm 29:10) A flood is a scary thing, and I think David wants us to notice where the LORD sits in relation to it. Then he adds, "the LORD is enthroned as King forever." (Psalm 29:10) Flood on one side, a King on His throne forever on the other.
Clouds feel right for a throne, I'll admit. But David says something different: "The LORD sits enthroned over the flood…" (Psalm 29:10) Flood is the word he uses here, friend.
Mountains are a natural thing to reach for, so I see the pull. But the word David uses here is flood: "The LORD sits enthroned over the flood…" (Psalm 29:10) That's the one that fills the blank.
True, baker. David says, "the LORD is enthroned as King forever." (Psalm 29:10) Forever is a long time, longer than anything I've ever left in an oven. The psalm doesn't say His reign will end.

This one is true, friend. The psalm says, "the LORD is enthroned as King forever." (Psalm 29:10) David doesn't give His kingship an end date. After all that thunder and fire, that's where the voice lands.

Close, but that one's false, friend. At the start, David asks the heavenly beings to ascribe "…glory and strength." to the LORD. (Psalm 29:1) At the end it's the other direction, and it's about "His people": "The LORD gives His people strength…" (Psalm 29:11) Nothing there says He gives strength to the heavenly beings.

False is right, baker. The psalm ends with, "The LORD gives His people strength; the LORD blesses His people with peace." (Psalm 29:11) The strength goes to His people, not to the heavenly beings. At the start, David calls on the heavenly beings to ascribe strength to the LORD (Psalm 29:1).
That's right, baker. "the LORD blesses His people with peace." (Psalm 29:11) After all that thunder, fire and shaking, the very last word of the psalm is peace. I think that's a lovely way to end it.

Riches would be a nice ending, I won't lie, and my bakery budget agrees. But David doesn't say riches anywhere in this psalm. He says, "the LORD blesses His people with peace." (Psalm 29:11) After all that shaking and fire, peace is the last word he leaves them with.

Joy is a good word, and I can see why you reached for it. But David doesn't use it in this verse. He says, "the LORD blesses His people with peace." (Psalm 29:11) Peace is the last thing the psalm says.
